stories.topic: How Nighttime Lights Were Discovered as an Economic Proxy
stories.summary: US government satellites were taking nighttime photographs of the world for unrelated reasons. Clever analysts noticed by accident that they were picking up city lights — and that as a city grew successful, its light footprint expanded. This led to the conjecture that nighttime light could be a measurable proxy for economic activity, and an entire field was born from a side-effect of military imagery.
stories.insight: Major scientific fields often emerge from accidental observations on the margins of someone else's project. The lesson is to keep looking at your data with curiosity, even — especially — when you are looking for something else.

stories.topic: North Korea vs South Korea at Night
stories.summary: One of the most iconic images in the field is the satellite photo of the Korean peninsula at night. South Korea blazes with light; North Korea is a black hole. Ajay shows the same picture in 2012 and again in 2025 — the contrast has only grown. He calls this 'one of the most influential pictures in the history of the socialism question.'
stories.insight: A single image can settle an empirical debate that volumes of theory cannot. The question 'does socialism work?' has two great answers: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich, and a satellite photo of Korea at 1:30 AM. As Ajay quips, 'You should have tried it on hamsters first.'

stories.summary: Drawing simple maps and graphs of Bombay's nighttime light data, Ajay's team noticed a sharp collapse in radiance every July. They knew Bombay's GDP doesn't actually fall every July — but they also knew July is monsoon. NASA/NOAA's algorithm classifies days as cloudy or cloud-free in a binary way and discards cloudy days. The team realised that in a month with only 3 cloud-free days out of 31, those 3 days are themselves probably hazy with wisps of cloud, attenuating the signal. They proposed a conservative bias correction using the fraction of cloud-free days as a quality signal.
stories.insight: Local ground truth — 'we live in Bombay, we know there are no truly cloud-free days in July' — is the hidden engine of good empirical work. Without that intuition you trust the data too much; with it, you can spot a bias even great institutions like NASA missed. Half the battle in economics is measurement.

stories.summary: When the team finally tackled Russia, the first surprise was practical: Russia is so big — the largest country on Earth by area — that the satellite imagery couldn't be loaded into a single computer's memory. They had to slice the country into provinces, and even the largest single province turned out bigger than India.
stories.insight: Scale changes problems qualitatively, not just quantitatively. Methods that 'just work' for India shatter on Russia, and that gap is itself information about why Russia is hard to govern, hard to study, and hard to fight.

stories.topic: The 1:30 AM Sun in St Petersburg
stories.summary: The VIIRS satellite captures images at 1:30 AM local time — perfect for India, useless for high-latitude St Petersburg in summer, where the sun is still shining at that hour. Ajay had to discover this as a methodological problem and design around it. He uses it as a parable for his core slogan: 'Love your data deeply. Look deep in her eyes. Without that you will never make progress.'
stories.insight: Methods imported from one geography do not automatically transfer. Globalisation of techniques without sensitivity to local conditions is itself a form of garbage-in-garbage-out — even satellite data has a cultural context.

stories.summary: Year after year of the Russia-Ukraine war passed and Ajay kept thinking, 'surely some European lab will publish a nighttime-lights paper on Russia.' None did. Then in 2024, Swedish intelligence released a public statement noting a sharp decline of nighttime lights over Russia in 2023. That was the trigger: 'Intelligence agencies are using nighttime lights data and the damn academics are not. They have skin in the game.' Ajay decided his under-resourced team would do it themselves.
stories.insight: Sometimes the only way to get a public-good piece of research done is to do it yourself, even when better-resourced labs are 'obviously' going to. Skin in the game beats abundance of resources; the people who need an answer to act will outpace the people who only need an answer to publish.

stories.topic: The Aurora Borealis Problem in Ukraine
stories.summary: Among the methodological surprises in studying Russia and Ukraine: the aurora borealis dumps astonishing amounts of light into the satellite over Ukraine in 2019. The team had to explicitly account for it as a bias source — light that has nothing to do with economic activity but pollutes the signal.
stories.insight: Every measurement domain has its 'dragons' — phenomena that look like signal but are actually noise, only visible if you're paying attention. Discipline in research is largely the practice of cataloguing your dragons.

recommendations.item: Shedding Light on the Russia-Ukraine War
recommendations.creator: Rounak Hande, Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah & Susan Thomas
recommendations.context: The xKDR working paper that uses nighttime lights data to estimate the state of the Russian wartime economy.
recommendations.reason: The substantive paper that gives this episode its title — finds that aggregate Russian radiance in January 2025 is roughly equal to January 2019, with damage concentrated near the Ukraine and EU borders and the centre of mass shifting 245 km eastward.

recommendations.item: But Clouds Got in My Way: Bias and Bias Correction of VIIRS Nighttime Lights Data in the Presence of Clouds
recommendations.creator: Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah, Anshul Tayal & Susan Thomas
recommendations.context: The methods paper documenting and fixing the cloud-induced bias in NASA/NOAA's nighttime lights data.
recommendations.reason: The foundation underneath the Russia paper. Argues that nobody in the world should use raw NASA/NOAA nighttime lights any more — they should use the bias-corrected version. Title is a Joni Mitchell allusion ('Both Sides Now').

recommendations.creator: xKDR Forum
recommendations.context: xKDR's open-source Julia package implementing the bias-correction methodology.
recommendations.reason: Made fully public so any researcher anywhere can apply the same techniques to any country, change parameters, and reproduce or extend the work. An embodiment of the 'spirit of inquiry' Amit praises in the episode.

recommendations.item: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich
recommendations.creator: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
recommendations.context: Solzhenitsyn's spare novella on a day in a Soviet labour camp.
recommendations.reason: Cited as 'answer one' to the question 'does socialism work?' — the satellite image of North Korea vs South Korea at night being 'answer two.' Both are devastating in their compression.

recommendations.creator: Joni Mitchell
recommendations.context: Joni Mitchell's classic song about looking at clouds — and life — from both sides.
recommendations.reason: The source of the title 'But Clouds Got in My Way' (paraphrasing the lyric 'But now they only block the sun / They rain and snow on everyone'). Ajay calls out to Joni Mitchell fans to listen.

recommendations.item: What Should India Do? (Episode 114 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A recent EIE episode on Indian engagement with America and China.
recommendations.reason: Referenced for the principle invoked in this episode — that strategic action requires deep understanding of your adversaries (Hitler did not understand America; this episode's MAGA-isolationist America is similarly poorly understood).

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode laying out how modern war has changed.
recommendations.reason: Provides the framing of standoff weapons that lets this episode interpret the ring of damage deep inside Russia — Ukraine's deep-strike capability is precisely the 'future of war' phenomenon predicted there.

core_ideas.concept: Nighttime Lights as a Proxy for Economic Activity
core_ideas.explanation: VIIRS satellites photograph Earth every night at 1:30 AM, with each pixel covering about 700-800 metres square. Brighter pixels correspond to more streetlights, compound walls, all-night petrol stations, restaurants, motorbikes — all the apparatus of urban prosperity. The relationship is monotonic in GDP (richer places are brighter) but not linear, and not stationary. Once correctly handled, it gives city-level monthly economic data — something no traditional statistical system can match.
core_ideas.quote: The bird in the sky is a glorious improvement of measurement. But we've got to be thoughtful — we can't just blindly roll out these measures.

core_ideas.explanation: Economists got over-excited and treated nighttime lights as a plug-in replacement for GDP. It isn't. It's a proxy for economic activity, but with structural limits: a one-storey building's light leaks to the sky, a five-storey building's mostly doesn't (so vertical urbanisation is undercounted); LED adoption cuts measured light by 34% even as prosperity rises (LEDs emit at frequencies the atmosphere blocks); and at very high incomes, doubling your wealth no longer doubles your lighting (Switzerland and the US look similar from orbit).
core_ideas.quote: When your income doubles, is your lighting going to double? No, you are done. You have reached the zenith of human prosperity where there is no possibility of your buying any more lights.

core_ideas.explanation: The core intellectual ethic Ajay preaches: half the battle in economics is measuring something correctly. Theorising and analysis come after. Researchers who lazily download data and run regressions ('garbage in, garbage out') waste the lifetimes of everyone downstream. The discipline is to either gain extreme mastery over a measure's strengths and limitations or refuse to use it.
core_ideas.quote: You must be passionate about measurement. You have to really wage war on measurement. Half the battle is measuring something correctly.

core_ideas.explanation: NASA/NOAA classify each night as cloudy (discard) or cloud-free (keep), then average the keeps for a monthly figure. But in a city like Bombay where July has 28 cloudy days and only 3 cloud-free, those 3 'cloud-free' days are likely still hazy. The fraction of cloud-free days is itself a quality signal — low fractions mean the surviving data is biased downward. xKDR's correction uses this fraction to undo the bias, deliberately conservative (under-correcting) so that no user need worry about over-correction errors.
core_ideas.quote: There is no case for anybody in the world to use the traditional NASA NOAA data. They should use our bias correction.

core_ideas.explanation: Long-term wars of attrition are won by economies, not battlefields. Hitler's fatal misunderstanding was declaring war on America after Pearl Harbor — once American production mobilised, the war was arithmetically over. Japan, an island, was strangled by US naval interdiction of its raw-material sea lanes. Today, Ukraine doesn't need to produce — Europe (whose economy dwarfs Russia's Italy-sized economy) produces for it. Russia, with only North Korea as patron, is essentially alone economically.
core_ideas.quote: Russia is an Italy-sized economy and Germany and France and the UK are just in a different league altogether when it comes to production.

core_ideas.concept: The Three Hammers on Russia's Economy
core_ideas.explanation: First, brain drain: 1-2 million of the most educated and rich people fled Russia at the start of the war. Second, Western sanctions cut off purchases, payments, and money flows, well-enforced by the West, leakily by others. Third, military mobilisation reorients production from civilian to military goods — more guns, less butter — which shrinks the civilian economy even as total output stays flat. The civilian economy is being eaten to feed the war.

core_ideas.concept: The End of the Strategic Hinterland
core_ideas.explanation: In WWII, Soviet factories were moved deep into the interior because German bombers couldn't reach. Today, Ukraine's standoff weapons can hit targets 100, 500, 1000, even 2000 km inside Russia (roughly Delhi-to-Bangalore distance). There is no longer any safe industrial backfield. The implication for future wars — Ajay names Taiwan explicitly — is that hundreds of kilometres inside the Chinese coast would be the kill zone if Xi Jinping invades.
core_ideas.quote: Imagine there is a war going on at Delhi, but there are deep strike weapons coming and hitting near the Karnataka Tamil Nadu border. That is the footprint of the kind of long-range weapons Ukraine is now bringing to the table.

core_ideas.concept: Three Findings From Russian Nighttime Lights
core_ideas.explanation: Comparing January 2019 to January 2025 (both cloud-free winter months) yields three insights. (1) Aggregate Russian radiance is essentially flat — economy not collapsed, not grown. (2) The Ukraine border lights up red on a growth-rate map: deep-strike weapons are visibly damaging Russia hundreds of kilometres in. The Baltic-state-facing border also dims, from sanctions, not war. The eastern border with Central Asia is fine — those countries don't enforce sanctions. (3) The centre of mass of the Russian economy has shifted 245 km eastward — production has moved away from war and from sanctioned trade.

NASA, NOAA, ESA, JAXA produce decades-long, regularly-updated, freely-downloadable global satellite datasets. This is a statistical system without the institutional complexity of a CSO walking the country. Ajay marvels at it as 'a great public good produced with government money,' worrying half-jokingly that if Trump notices, he might demand compensation. The xKDR team contributes back in the same spirit — open papers, open data, open Julia package.
core_ideas.quote: We shouldn't say this too loudly because if Donald Trump is an enthusiastic watcher of Everything is Everything, he will complain that these are global public goods and the US government is not being compensated for doing these good things.

core_ideas.concept: Skin in the Game vs. Academic Inertia
core_ideas.explanation: For years Ajay assumed European labs would study Russia's wartime economy with nighttime lights — surely with 500 labs in the field, somebody. They didn't. Swedish intelligence published a finding before any academic did. The asymmetry: intelligence agencies need the answer to act, academics need it to publish, and need-to-act beats need-to-publish every time. The lesson: if you want a public good produced, sometimes you must produce it yourself even when 'someone else obviously will.'
core_ideas.quote: Intelligence agencies in advanced economies are using nighttime lights data and the damn academics are not. They have skin in the game.

core_ideas.concept: Unconventional Metrics for the Real World
core_ideas.explanation: GDP and other traditional aggregates miss most of what matters about a society. Amit's example: rising divorce rates as a metric of women's empowerment to leave bad marriages. From Metrics of Empowerment: who orders more from the groceries app? Nighttime lights itself is the same trick at scale. The episode closes by promising a future EIE devoted to creative proxies for the parts of life — 'how we love, how we have sex, how we write poems' — that conventional data misses entirely.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's acrostic poem 'Nighttime Lights' (NIGHTTIMELIGHTS as the first letters), in iambic tetrameter, opening the episode — and his deadpan 'I can see that you aren't tearing up, this is very sad. Maybe we should make AI make you cry.'
Ajay on socialism, after showing the Korea-at-night image: 'You should have tried it on hamsters first.'

Ajay on why nighttime lights cap out at high incomes: 'When your income doubles, is your lighting going to double? No, you are done. You have reached the zenith of human prosperity.' Amit's straight-man addition: 'Also, double of zero is zero.'

Amit on 'many a slip between cup and lip' — 'I drop tea all the time on the way from the cup to the lip.' Then: 'I can also imagine Vivian Richards is playing against India and he's about to raise his cup to his lip when suddenly he sees Sunil Gavaskar Chetan Chauhan etcetera etcetera...'

Amit's quatrain triggered by the word 'incandescent': 'I told her she was incandescent / when I met her for a lark / She looked at me with twinkling eyes / and said I was too...' (sparking the running 'Ajay, you inspire poetry in me' bit).

Amit's third quatrain, triggered by Ajay's call to 'love your data': 'I said to her, I'll treasure you / I love you bit by bit / first, my love I'll measure you / to make sure that...' Ajay: 'You weren't a good economist at twenty or thirty or forty — it took some time.'
Ajay on Russian gas flaring: 'Russia is a communist country, they don't know how to handle the gas.'
Ajay on the show being secretly watched in the Kremlin: 'January is the time to peek into the Kremlin and look at what Putin is doing on his morning morning walk.'
Ajay worrying that if Trump watches EIE, he'll demand the US be compensated for NASA's free public-good data: 'Shh.'
Amit's title of his sub-paper: 'great minds think alike' — riffing on Ajay's revelation that the Russia paper is called Shedding Light on the Russia-Ukraine War.
Amit on America's self-comprehension: 'I don't think anybody understands America. I don't think America understands America.'
Amit on his economist friends: 'The reason you're my favorite economist friend is because you use words with spark poetry in me... no offense to you' — followed by 'Oh wait, I have none.'
Freddy, the on-screen mascot, named after Freddie Bassiya, named after Freddie Hayek — the show's running riff on Friedrich Hayek and Freddie Mercury collapsing into one dog.
'But Clouds Got in My Way' — title of the methods paper, paraphrasing Joni Mitchell's 'Both Sides Now' (which is linked in the show notes specifically for fans to enjoy the allusion).
The North Korea / South Korea satellite image — described as 'one of the most influential pictures in the history of the socialism question.'
One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich — Solzhenitsyn invoked as the literary 'answer one' to the question 'does socialism work?', with the Korea image as 'answer two.'

CMIE (Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy) — Ajay's standard for empirical rigor: 'CMIE levels of training' means 'don't casually jump into using data; either you have extreme mastery on its limitations or you don't use it at all.'
Bandra West vs Bandra East — Ajay's go-to local sanity check for any economic measurement methodology: if your data doesn't say Bandra West is brighter than Bandra East, something is amiss.
Hitler declaring war on the United States the day after Pearl Harbor — Ajay's canonical example of strategic blunder through failure to understand your adversary.
